candidates.label: Myra archaeological site
candidates.support: A Lycian city with a harbor used by grain ships from Alexandria. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site; Wikidata's own record places it within Demre district, Türkiye.

summary.text: Myra was a city of ancient Lycia, a few kilometers from the coast, with a harbor used by ships from Egypt and Cyprus. Acts records that the centurion guarding Paul as a prisoner transferred him and the other prisoners at Myra onto a grain ship of Alexandria bound for Italy.

history.text: The Roman historian Cassius Dio records that in AD 43, after the Lycians revolted and killed some Romans, the emperor Claudius reduced them to servitude and incorporated them into the prefecture of Pamphylia. Lycia's exact status for the following decades is unclear: the Roman biographer Suetonius records that the emperor Vespasian made a province of Lycia, implying it had freedom again by his reign, while a translator's note to the Roman historian Tacitus's Histories states that Galatia, Pamphylia and Lycia already formed one province together by AD 69.

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia states that Myra was at first less important than the nearby Lycian city of Patara, but later became a leading port for ships from Egypt and Cyprus, and that the Eastern Roman emperor Theodosius II made it the capital of the province. In Christian tradition, which the encyclopedia's article on Lycia records, Myra is honored as the home city of the bishop Nicholas, now remembered as a patron saint of sailors and traditionally said to be buried in a church on the road to the port.

scripture.textWEB: When we had sailed across the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia.

politicalHistory.note: The Roman historian Cassius Dio says the emperor Claudius "incorporated them in the prefecture of Pamphylia," not that Lycia became its own province; the Roman biographer Suetonius separately records that the emperor Vespasian made a province of Lycia, implying it had freedom again by his reign, and a translator's note to the Roman historian Tacitus's Histories (2.9) states that "Galatia, Pamphylia, and Lycia" formed one province together by AD 69, leaving Lycia's exact status across this span unclear.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Lycia and Pamphylia
